title: GATE-AD: Graph Attention Network Encoding for Few-Shot Industrial Visual Anomaly Detection
claim: Model normality by reconstructing masked patch features from spatial-neighbor context with a graph attention encoder aligned in a latent space.
layout: Single wide panel, left-to-right flow with bottom return loop; color-coded train/inference arrows
description: A wide architecture diagram that reads left to right. On the left, a green dashed box holds the normal support set of screw images, and a red dashed box holds the query image. Both go into a frozen DINO block (snowflake icon), which outputs a grid of patch features X. The features are arranged on a spatial neighbor graph with a highlighted local neighborhood. A masked graph with 'M' nodes follows. Next comes a stacked GAT encoder (Layer 1 to R) with a star-shaped attention diagram and the update equation. Its output H^R feeds a lower green region on representation alignment. That region has two small MLPs, q(X) and g(H^R), a 3D latent-space scatter with vectors z_i and z̃_i, and a training loss box (L_SCE). Green arrows mark training and red arrows mark inference. Inference ends in interpolation and a pixel anomaly heatmap on the screw. A legend sits at the bottom right.
caption: General architecture of the proposed masked, representation-aligned GAT encoding scheme for FS-IVAD.
abstract: Few-Shot Industrial Visual Anomaly Detection (FS-IVAD) is a critical task in modern manufacturing, where automated product inspection systems must identify rare defects using only a handful of normal, defect-free training samples. Existing approaches typically model normality by assessing each patch largely through its individual appearance, e.g., through similarity to stored normal features, reconstruction from support samples, or distance from a learned normal representation. This paper introduces GATE-AD, whose key contribution is to instead model few-shot normality through local contextual relations: a patch is considered normal when it can be consistently recovered from its learned dependencies with its spatial neighbors. To realize this formulation, frozen self-supervised ViT patch tokens are organized on a spatial neighbor graph and processed by a Graph Attention Network (GAT), while representation alignment and a Scaled Cosine Error (SCE) objective enable reconstruction-based anomaly scoring. Node masking and attention dropout further regularize learning in the low-shot regime. On MVTec AD, VisA, and MPDD, GATE-AD achieves strong detection and localization performance across $1$- to $8$-shot settings, attaining the highest image-level AUROC in $10$ of $12$ settings and the highest image-level AP in $8$ of $12$ settings under a unified evaluation protocol, while also achieving the lowest inference latency among the compared methods. In order to facilitate reproducibility and further research, the source code of GATE-AD is available at https://github.com/gthpapadopoulos/GATE-AD.
